```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A lag sequential model is defined by two choices that precede any test: the
distance at which events are paired, and the set of transitions the model
treats as possible. The lag $\ell$ fixes the pairing. At $\ell = 1$ each event
is paired with the next one; at $\ell = 2$ with the one after that; at
$\ell = -1$ with the one before it. Comparing lags tells whether a sequential
dependency is immediate and short-lived or persists over several steps
(Bakeman & Quera, 2011). The set of possible transitions fixes the reference
model. Some transitions cannot occur by construction, the standard case being
a coding scheme in which a state cannot follow itself. Those cells are
*structural zeros*: they are empty because they are impossible, not because
they are avoided, and the independence model has to be fitted to the
remaining cells only. Expected counts then come from the quasi-independence
model fitted by iterative proportional fitting (Wickens, 1989), and residuals
use the design-matrix form of Christensen (1997).

This guide covers both choices: single fits at a lag other than 1, negative
lags, lag profiles with `lsa_lags()` and `lag_profile()`, and structural zeros
declared with `loops = FALSE` or an explicit `structural_zeros` matrix. The
basic model and its reading verbs are introduced in
[the LSA vignette](lsa.html); the other engines, which do not support
structural zeros, are described in [the engines guide](engines.html).

```{r package}
library(lagdynamics)
```

## Data

- **`engagement`**: weekly engagement states (`Active`, `Average`,
  `Disengaged`) of 138 students over 15 weeks, one row per student. Two rows
  are entirely missing, so fits use 136 sequences.
- **`group_regulation`**: coded regulation actions in 2,000 collaborative
  learning sessions, one row per session and one column per ordered time
  point (`T1` to `T26`). Nine states: `adapt`, `cohesion`, `consensus`,
  `coregulate`, `discuss`, `emotion`, `monitor`, `plan`, `synthesis`.

Transitions are counted within a sequence only, at every lag: a pair never
spans two students or two sessions.

## A single fit at another lag

The `lag` argument of `lsa()` sets the distance between the paired events.
At lag 2 the model asks whether the state two weeks later depends on the
current one.

```{r lag-two}
lsa(engagement, lag = 2)
```

The lag-2 table has 1,603 transitions against 1,734 at lag 1, because each
sequence contributes one pair fewer. The dependency survives the extra week:
eight of the nine cells depart from independence, and the three
self-transitions remain the strongest over-represented cells (Active to
Active, $z = 18.7$). A student's engagement two weeks ahead is still predicted
by this week's state.

## Predecessors: negative lags

A negative lag pairs each event with an earlier one. At `lag = -1` the row
`from -> to` counts how often an event in `from` was *preceded* by `to`, so
the table answers the question "what came before this state?".

```{r lag-minus-one}
transitions(lsa(engagement, lag = -1))
```

The lag $-1$ table is the transpose of the lag 1 table. The row
`Average -> Active` counts 176 events in `Average` preceded by `Active`,
which are the same 176 pairs as `Active -> Average` at lag 1, with the same
adjusted residual ($z = -11.3$). What changes is the conditioning of `prob`:
at lag $-1$ it is the probability of the predecessor given the current state.
Of all events in `Average`, 23.1% were preceded by `Active`; at lag 1 the
same number appears as `prob_col`, the share of `Average` events that came
from `Active`. Negative lags do not add new tests to a single fit; they
re-express the table from the target's side, and they make a lag profile read
symmetrically around the present event.

## Lag profiles

`lsa_lags()` fits the same model at several lags in one call. Its print
method reports how many transitions are significant at each lag.

```{r engagement-lags}
engagement_lags <- lsa_lags(engagement, lags = c(-2, -1, 1, 2, 3))
engagement_lags
```

Most of the table departs from independence at every lag from $-2$ to 3, so
the engagement process has a long memory. The lag 0 fit is left out on
purpose: at lag 0 each event is paired with itself, so the table is diagonal
and every cell trivially departs from independence.

`lag_profile()` follows a single transition across lags as a one-row-per-lag
table.

```{r active-profile}
lag_profile(engagement, from = "Active", to = "Active", lags = 1:5)
```

Staying `Active` remains strongly over-represented five weeks ahead
($z = 13.9$ at lag 5, against 21.7 at lag 1). The decline is gradual and not
strictly monotone (16.0 at lag 3, 16.3 at lag 4). Engagement in this cohort
is a durable state, not a week-to-week fluctuation.

The `transitions()` verb reads the multi-lag result with the same filters as
a single fit. The call below keeps the over-represented transitions at lags 1
to 3, strongest first within each lag.

```{r engagement-over}
transitions(lsa_lags(engagement, lags = 1:3), direction = "over",
            sort = "strength")
```

The self-transitions are the only over-represented cells at lags 1 and 2. At
lag 3 one more cell appears, `Average -> Disengaged` ($z = 2.52$): an average
week raises the chance of a disengaged week three weeks later, an effect that
is absent at lag 1 ($z = 0.18$, shown above in transposed form as
`Disengaged -> Average` at lag $-1$). Delayed effects of this kind are invisible to
a lag 1 analysis.

The collaborative regulation data behave differently.

```{r regulation-lags}
regulation_lags <- lsa_lags(group_regulation, lags = 1:3)
regulation_lags
lag_profile(regulation_lags, from = "emotion", to = "cohesion")
lag_profile(regulation_lags, from = "plan", to = "consensus")
```

The number of significant transitions falls from 72 of 81 at lag 1 to 41 at
lag 2 and 10 at lag 3. The sequential structure of these sessions is local:
an action constrains the next action, much less the one after. The
`emotion -> cohesion` transition, the strongest of the lag 1 table
($z = 58.2$), turns slightly under-represented at lag 2 ($z = -2.35$) and is
indistinguishable from independence at lag 3. `plan -> consensus` changes
sign: over-represented at lag 1 ($z = 8.53$), under-represented at lag 2
($z = -3.62$). A lag 1 network of these data describes immediate responses,
not longer chains.

A residual heatmap of the lag 2 fit shows which dependencies remain once the
immediate response is skipped.

```{r heatmap-lag-two, fig.height = 5}
plot(lsa(group_regulation, lag = 2))
```

Two actions apart, `discuss -> adapt` ($z = 14.26$) and `plan -> plan`
($z = 10.11$) are the strongest over-represented cells, and
`consensus -> coregulate` is the most avoided ($z = -10.83$). The residuals
are about a quarter of the size of the lag 1 residuals, which reach 58.2.

## Declaring structural zeros

Three cells of the `group_regulation` table are empty: `adapt -> adapt`,
`adapt -> synthesis` and `synthesis -> synthesis`. Sorting the transitions by
count puts them in the last three rows.

```{r empty-cells}
regulation_fit <- lsa(group_regulation)
transitions(regulation_fit, sort = "count") |> tail(3)
```

Under ordinary independence each empty cell is a significant avoidance
($z$ from $-3.32$ to $-4.31$), because the margins predict between 10.6 and
17.6 transitions there. Whether that is a finding depends on the coding
scheme. If these transitions are possible but never chosen, the residuals are
the result. If the scheme makes them impossible, the residuals are an
artefact, and the cells must be removed from the model rather than tested.

The `structural_zeros` argument takes a $K \times K$ matrix with 0 for a
forbidden cell and 1 for an estimable one. Rows and columns follow the state
order that the fit reports (`nodes(regulation_fit)` lists it; states are
sorted alphabetically). The matrix below is built from the names of the
forbidden transitions.

```{r structural-matrix}
states <- c("adapt", "cohesion", "consensus", "coregulate", "discuss",
            "emotion", "monitor", "plan", "synthesis")
forbidden <- c("adapt -> adapt", "adapt -> synthesis",
               "synthesis -> synthesis")
allowed <- outer(states, states,
                 \(from, to) 1 * !(paste(from, "->", to) %in% forbidden))
allowed
```

Fitting with the matrix switches the classical engine to the
quasi-independence model.

```{r structural-fit}
constrained_fit <- lsa(group_regulation, structural_zeros = allowed)
constrained_fit
tests(regulation_fit)
tests(constrained_fit)
transitions(constrained_fit, sort = "count") |> tail(3)
```

Three things change. First, the forbidden cells have an expected count of 0
and no residual, p-value or lift, so they are no longer flagged: 69 of 81
transitions are significant instead of 72. Second, the expected counts of the
remaining cells are refitted so that the row and column totals are still
matched with the forbidden cells empty, which moves the residuals of the
other cells slightly (`emotion -> cohesion` goes from 58.2 to 58.3). Third, the tablewise test loses one degree of freedom per forbidden
cell: $G^2$ falls from 13,204 on 64 df to 13,116 on 61 df. The substantive
conclusions about the other 78 transitions do not change; the three avoidance
"findings" are gone.

The forbidden rows still show `yules_q` and `kappa` values ($-1$, with
`kappa_p` below 0.001). These columns are computed from the observed counts
of the full table and do not use the structural-zero model, so on a forbidden
cell they carry no information and are ignored.

## Forbidding self-transitions with `loops = FALSE`

The most common structural-zero pattern is the diagonal. When a coding scheme
merges consecutive identical codes, for example a dialogue coded turn by turn
where a new code starts only when the act changes, a state can never follow
itself. `loops = FALSE` declares the whole diagonal forbidden without building
a matrix. The model assumes that these cells are empty in the data; when
transitions do fall in a forbidden cell, `lsa()` warns with the condition
`lagdynamics_structural_zero_counts`, because the data contradict the
declaration, and leaves those transitions out of the fit: the
quasi-independence model is fitted to the possible cells, with the margins of
those cells (Bakeman & Quera, 1995). Every
state repeats in the bundled datasets (459 `Active -> Active` transitions in
`engagement`), so they are not candidates for this model; the example uses a
small count table of three dialogue acts with an empty diagonal, which
`lsa()` accepts directly.

```{r turns}
turns <- matrix(c( 0, 34, 18,
                  27,  0, 41,
                  25, 30,  0),
                nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
                dimnames = list(c("Question", "Answer", "Feedback"),
                                c("Question", "Answer", "Feedback")))
turns
```

Fitted under ordinary independence, the empty diagonal distorts the whole
table.

```{r turns-independence}
transitions(lsa(turns))
tests(lsa(turns))
```

Eight of the nine cells are significant. The three empty diagonal cells are
strongly "avoided" ($z$ from $-5.59$ to $-8.01$), and to keep the margins, the
model spreads part of every margin over the diagonal and the off-diagonal expected counts fall below the observed ones, so five of the six real
transitions appear over-represented. The tablewise test rejects independence
($G^2 = 149$, df = 4). All of this follows from the coding rule, not from the
dialogue.

```{r turns-quasi}
transitions(lsa(turns, loops = FALSE))
tests(lsa(turns, loops = FALSE))
```

Under quasi-independence the diagonal is excluded and no transition is
significant. With three states and a forbidden diagonal the model has a
single degree of freedom, which is why all six residuals have the same size
($|z| = 1.87$, $p = 0.062$): the one remaining question is whether the
dialogue cycles in one direction. The signs give the answer the data lean
towards, `Question -> Answer -> Feedback -> Question` more often than the
reverse, but the tablewise test ($G^2 = 3.49$, df = 1, $p = 0.062$) does not
support it at the 0.05 level. The independence fit reported a strong
sequential structure; the correct model finds none.

The expected counts of the quasi-independence model come from iterative
proportional fitting, available on its own as `lsa_ipf()`. It takes a count
matrix and a 0/1 structure matrix of the same shape.

```{r ipf}
lsa_ipf(turns, structure = 1 - diag(3))
```

The fitted table is the `expected` column of the `loops = FALSE` fit
(31, 21, 30, 34, 22 and 37 off the diagonal, 0 on it): its row and column
totals equal those of `turns` and its diagonal is 0. The fit converged in 22
row-and-column passes. `loops = FALSE` and an explicit `structural_zeros`
matrix combine: with both, the diagonal of the matrix is zeroed as well.

## What changes with structural zeros

| Quantity | Independence | Quasi-independence (structural zeros) |
|---|---|---|
| Expected count | $R_i C_j / N$ | IPF fit with forbidden cells fixed at 0, margins matched |
| Residual | Haberman adjusted residual | Christensen residual $(O - E)/\sqrt{E(1 - h)}$, $h$ from the hat matrix of the row and column design |
| Forbidden cell | tested like any other | `expected = 0`; `adj_res`, `p`, `lift` are `NA`; never significant |
| Degrees of freedom | $(K - 1)^2$ | estimable cells minus rank of the design; $(K - 1)^2 - s$ for $s$ forbidden cells in a non-degenerate pattern |
| `yules_q`, `kappa` | from observed counts | unchanged: still from observed counts, not part of the structural model |

The two residual formulas coincide when no cell is forbidden. Structural
zeros are supported by the classical engine only; the two-cell,
bidirectional and dominance engines stop with an error of class
`lagdynamics_unsupported_option`. Declare a structural zero only when the
coding scheme rules a transition out. An empty cell that could have occurred
is a result to report, not a cell to remove.

## References

Bakeman, R., & Quera, V. (2011). *Sequential analysis and observational
methods for the behavioral sciences*. Cambridge University Press.

Christensen, R. (1997). *Log-linear models and logistic regression* (2nd
ed.). Springer.

Wickens, T. D. (1989). *Multiway contingency tables analysis for the social
sciences*. Lawrence Erlbaum.
